title: Painting the Hills of Valparaíso
focus: Present perfect and present perfect continuous
paragraphs: Valparaíso is a port city in Chile, and its hills are full of colour. Walk up any steep street and you will find murals on stairs, walls and even garage doors. Some paintings are huge and some are tiny, but almost all of them tell a story about the neighbourhood. Visitors come from all over the world to take photos.

Camila Rojas, a nineteen-year-old art student, has been painting there for three years. 'At first I was nervous because I didn't have permission,' she says. 'Now the owners often ask me to paint their walls. One old man even brought me a cup of tea every afternoon while I was working.'

Not everyone is happy, though. Some residents think that graffiti makes the streets look dirty, and every year the city spends millions of pesos cleaning walls. To solve the problem, the council has started a new programme. Young artists can now apply for an official wall, and neighbours vote for the best design.

Camila's latest mural shows a girl flying a kite above the port. It took her two weeks to finish, and she has already received invitations from two other cities. 'People think painting is just a hobby,' she says. 'For me it is a way to say thank you to the place where I grew up.'

If the programme works, other cities may copy the idea. Camila hopes so. She is saving money for a course in Santiago next year, and in the meantime she is planning a mural about the sea. Her advice to beginners is simple: ask the neighbours first, and bring a ladder.

title: Two Weeks Far from Home
paragraphs: 3 March. I have been in Auckland for exactly two weeks, and I still can't believe it. My host family is very kind. The mother, Hine, works as a nurse, and the father, Tom, teaches music. They have two children, a boy called Rua and a girl called Mere.

School is very different from my school in Puebla. Here the teachers use their first names, and the lessons are less formal. At first I felt shy, but my classmates have helped me a lot. Yesterday a girl called Aroha invited me to join the volleyball team.

The hardest thing is the accent. People speak quickly, and I often have to ask them to repeat things. Last Tuesday I wanted to buy a sandwich, but I didn't understand the question 'Would you like that toasted?' I just said 'yes' and got a very hot sandwich. It was delicious, so I think my mistake was lucky!

I miss my family and my dog, Canela. I have called my mum three times this week, and every time she asks if I am eating enough. I told her not to worry. Hine cooks big dinners, and I have already tried lamb, sweet potato and a dessert with cream and fruit that I can't pronounce.

Tomorrow I am starting a project about local birds with Rua. We are going to the beach at six in the morning, so I need to sleep early. I think this exchange is going to change me. I am more independent than before, and I haven't been homesick today. Good night, diary!

title: The Dog Who Disappeared on a Rainy Saturday
paragraphs: It was a rainy Saturday in Guadalajara when Itzel noticed that something was wrong. She was washing the dishes and listening to the radio when she realised that the house was too quiet. Bruno, her old brown dog, wasn't sleeping under the table. The back gate was open.

Itzel put on her coat and ran outside. She searched the street, the park and the bakery on the corner while the rain was getting heavier. Nobody had seen him. When she came home, her brother Rodrigo was making posters on his laptop. 'We will find him,' he said, but his voice didn't sound sure.

They printed twenty posters and walked around the neighbourhood until it was dark. A boy on a bicycle told them that he had seen a brown dog near the market, but when they got there, the stalls were already closed. Itzel went to bed late and slept badly. She kept thinking about Bruno alone in the cold.

On Sunday morning the phone rang while they were having breakfast. A woman called Señora Lupe said that a dog had been sitting outside her flower shop since dawn. 'He has a blue collar,' she said. 'And he is eating my flowers!' Itzel started to laugh and cry at the same time.

Ten minutes later, Bruno was in the kitchen, wet and happy. Rodrigo gave him a big bowl of food while Itzel dried him with a towel. Later they paid for the flowers and thanked Señora Lupe, who didn't mind at all. Now the gate has a new lock, and Bruno wears a tag with their phone number on it.

title: Review: 'Odd Jobs', a Podcast for Curious Minds
paragraphs: If you are looking for a podcast that is both funny and useful, try 'Odd Jobs'. Every week the hosts, Priya Nair and Diego Salas, interview someone with an unusual career. The episodes last about thirty minutes, so they are perfect for a bus ride or a walk.

My favourite episode was about a woman who tests mattresses for a living. At first I thought she was joking, but she explained that she lies on each bed for hours and writes detailed reports. I was surprised to learn how much science is involved. Another episode, about a man who repairs church clocks, was less exciting, although the sound effects were lovely.

What I like most about the show is the hosts. Priya asks clever questions, and Diego always finds a way to make guests relax. They never laugh at the guests, and they let them finish their sentences. Their English is clear and not too fast, which is helpful if you are still learning.

However, the podcast is not perfect. The adverts in the middle are too long, and some episodes have bad sound quality. Also, the guests sometimes use slang that is hard to follow, and the website has no written transcripts. It would be better if each episode had a short summary at the beginning.

Overall, I would give 'Odd Jobs' four stars out of five. It is not only entertaining but also full of real stories about people who love their work. Listen to the mattress episode first, and then decide for yourself. If you enjoy it, you will probably download every episode.

title: My First Surf Lesson in Máncora
paragraphs: This week I am finally doing something I have wanted to do for years: I am learning to surf in Máncora, a beach town in the north of Peru. I travelled by night bus from Piura with my cousin Elena, and we arrived tired but excited. The sea was warm, the sun was strong, and I had no idea what to expect.

Our instructor, Joel, gave us a simple rule on the first morning: 'If you are afraid, you will fall. If you relax, you will stand up.' He also told us to check the waves before every attempt. The first lesson cost forty soles, and the board and a T-shirt were included.

I fell more than twenty times that day. The water went into my nose, my arms hurt, and Elena laughed at me from the beach. Joel stayed calm. 'Don't look at your feet,' he kept saying. 'If you look at the beach, your body will follow.' I didn't believe him until the afternoon, when I finally stood up for three seconds.

Three seconds felt like an hour. I was so proud that I forgot to be tired. That night we ate fresh fish by the sea and made a plan for the next day. If the waves are small tomorrow, we will practise again, and if the weather is bad, we will rest and visit the market.

If you want to try surfing, my advice is simple. Choose a quiet beach, ask for a patient instructor and don't worry about looking silly. You will need sun cream, because the sun is stronger than you think. And if you fall, which you will, laugh and try again. That is exactly what I am going to do tomorrow.

title: A Weekend Without My Phone
paragraphs: Last weekend I made a deal with my friend Jonas: neither of us would touch our phones from Friday evening until Monday morning. I check my phone about a hundred times a day, so I thought it would be easy. It wasn't. On Friday night my hand kept reaching for a pocket that was empty.

At first I felt bored and a little anxious. I didn't know what time it was, and I couldn't listen to music while I was washing up. Then, on Saturday morning, I did something unusual: I took a long walk without any destination. I noticed a small bakery, a mural and a garden that I had never seen before, although I live only two streets away.

In the afternoon I read a book for three hours, which I haven't done since I was twelve. In the evening I cooked dinner for my parents, and we talked for a long time. My dad told me stories about his first job. Normally he eats in front of the television, so it felt special.

Of course, there were problems. A friend invited me to a party, but she couldn't reach me, so I missed it. Also, I didn't see an important message from my teacher about a change of room, and I arrived late on Monday. These things were annoying, but none of them was a disaster.

Would I do it again? Probably, but not every weekend. The experiment showed me that my phone is useful, but it also steals my attention. From now on I will turn it off during meals, and I will leave it in another room when I read. Jonas says he is going to do the same, although he admits that he cheated once to check the football score.

title: Saturdays at the Animal Shelter
paragraphs: Hi Cata,

Sorry I haven't written for a while. I have been very busy since I started volunteering at an animal shelter on Saturdays and Sundays. A friend from my class told me about it, and I decided to try it for one month. My parents were worried at first, but now they ask me about the animals every Sunday. Now I can't imagine stopping.

The shelter looks after about sixty dogs and thirty cats. My job is to clean the cages, give the animals food and water, and walk the dogs that are healthy enough. It is hard work, and my back hurts on Sunday night, but the dogs are so happy to see me that I forget about the pain. My favourite is a small white dog called Nube. She has been waiting for a family for eight months.

The shelter doesn't receive money from the government, so it depends on donations. Last week we organised a small sale of second-hand books and sold everything for 120 dollars. With that money, the shelter bought medicine for three sick puppies. We also have a Saturday routine: first the dogs, then the cats, and finally a cup of hot chocolate with the other volunteers. I felt really proud, and the manager, Doña Rosa, said that young volunteers are the heart of the place.

Why don't you come with me next weekend? You could meet Nube and see if you like the work. If you decide to adopt a pet one day, it is also a good way to learn about animals. Write back soon and tell me what you think.
Emilio

title: Vote for a Voice: A Campaign Speech
focus: First conditional and promises with will
paragraphs: Good morning, everyone. My name is Aisha Rahman, and I am in the final year of secondary school. Today I want to explain why I am asking for your vote for student representative.

First of all, let me be honest: I am not the most popular student in this school. I don't play football, and I am not in a band. However, I listen. For two months I have been asking students what they want to change, and more than two hundred people have answered my questionnaire.

The results were clear. Students are tired of the long queue in the canteen. They want a quiet room to study at lunchtime, and they would like more clubs. If you choose me, I will talk to the headteacher about these three things in my first week. I can't promise that she will say yes to everything, but I will fight for every idea.

I also have a plan for the clubs. If three students want to start a new club, they will only need one teacher to support them. Last year the chess club began exactly like this, and now it has forty members. Imagine what could happen with a photography club, a robotics club or a theatre group!

Finally, I want to say something to those of you who never vote because you think nothing will change. If you don't vote, nothing will change. If you vote, we have a chance. Please think about it carefully, talk to your friends, and choose the person you trust most. Thank you for listening.

title: From Seed to Cup: A Coffee Farm in Huila
paragraphs: Millions of people start their day with a cup of coffee, but few of them know how long the journey from seed to cup really is. In a small farm near Pitalito, in the department of Huila, Marisol Quintero shows visitors every step of the process. Her family has grown coffee there for three generations.

The story begins in a nursery, where the seeds are planted in small bags of soil. After several months, the young plants are moved to the field. Then comes the longest part: the farmers must wait for three or four years before the first cherries appear. 'Coffee teaches you patience,' Marisol says.

When the cherries turn red, they are picked by hand, one by one. Green cherries are not ready, so the pickers have to check every branch carefully. The cherries are then taken to a small machine that removes the skin. The seeds inside are washed and left in the sun to dry for several days.

After drying, the beans are sorted. Broken or ugly ones are thrown away, and only the best are kept for export. Finally, the beans are roasted. The longer they are roasted, the darker they become. Visitors can smell the roasting from the garden, and many say it is the best part of the tour.

At the end of the tour, everyone is invited to taste a cup of freshly made coffee. Marisol hopes that people will think about the farmers every time they drink it. 'Behind each cup there are many hands,' she says. 'If you understand that, you will enjoy it more.' Many of her guests are teenagers from the local schools, and some of them have decided to study agriculture.

title: Should I Tell My Friend the Truth?
paragraphs: Dear Marta,

My best friend, Dani, has written a song and wants to enter a talent contest at school. The problem is that the song isn't very good. The words are strange, and he sings out of tune. Yesterday he asked me, 'Do you think I'll win?' I said, 'Maybe,' because I didn't want to hurt him. If I told him the truth, he would be very sad. But if I say nothing, he might feel embarrassed on the stage. What should I do?
Nikolai
Dear Nikolai,

Thank you for your honest letter. It is clear that you care about Dani. Many people think that telling the truth and being kind are opposites, but they are not. If I were you, I would not say that the song is bad. I would talk about what is good and then suggest improvements.

Start with the positive. Perhaps the melody is nice, or perhaps he is very brave to perform in public. Then ask questions: 'Which part do you like best? Would you like some help with the words?' If you ask the right questions, he may discover the problems himself. You could also offer to listen to him sing three or four times before the contest and give small suggestions each time.

Remember that a friend who only says 'Great!' is not really helping. If Dani loses the contest and later discovers that you knew about the problems, he might feel disappointed in you. On the other hand, if you help him now, he will be grateful, even if he doesn't win. Good luck!
Marta
